Front: Optuna: what makes it smarter than grid/random search, and what's the term for the approach?
Back: It learns from completed trials to decide what to sample next, rather than sampling blindly. The approach is Bayesian optimization: build a probabilistic model of which hyperparameter values produce good scores, then sample new candidates weighted toward promising regions. Optuna's default sampler is TPE (Tree-structured Parzen Estimator). Grid/random search never use prior trial results.

Front: Optuna pruning: what is it and why does it help (beyond smart sampling)?
Back: Pruning kills an unpromising trial partway through training (based on intermediate results vs. other trials) instead of wasting a full training run on a bad config. It's a second efficiency lever on top of TPE's smarter sampling - sampling picks better configs, pruning stops wasting time on the bad ones that still get picked.

Front: Name efficiency metrics (not accuracy/F1) and give a case for accepting a less accurate model to win on one.
Back: Efficiency metrics: inference latency (time/prediction), throughput (predictions/sec), model size (MB / parameter count), compute footprint (FLOPs/memory). Case: edge/resource-constrained deployment (phone, embedded hardware, microcontroller robot) or real-time face recognition - a smaller, less accurate model that fits and runs in real time beats a more accurate one that can't run on the hardware at all.

Front: Flexible architecture design: why does it matter for hyperparameter tuning?
Back: Parameterizing architecture choices (layer sizes, counts, etc.) instead of hard-coding them is what makes them tunable - the search space for a tool like Optuna is defined over those parameters, so the architecture itself can be part of the optimization.
